original_question: Let s be an invertible exponent over a finite field L of odd characteristic, and call s nice when the differential multiplicity N(1, v) takes at most three values as v ranges over L. Numerical experiments in the paper found that all nice exponents s not equivalent to 1 over prime fields of characteristic p < 5000 come from the paradigmatic examples s = 3 and s = q - 2. Is that always the case over all finite fields of odd characteristic?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1, the paper’s 'nice exponent' conjecture, read together with the introductory consequences in Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 1.3.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the finite-field setting, the odd-characteristic restriction, the use of the differential counts N(1,v), the definition of 'nice' in terms of those counts taking at most three values, and the paper’s experimental observation that over prime fields the only nontrivial nice examples found were the classical exponents 3 and q-2.
missing_details: The paper’s actual open problem is not a classification of all nice exponents; it asks whether the value 2 must occur among the differential multiplicities of a nice exponent.
You need the exact definition N(u,v) = #{(x,y) in L^2 : x + y = u and x^s + y^s = v}.
You need the exact meaning of '2 is a differential multiplicity': there exists v in L such that N(1,v) = 2.
You should specify the ambient field as a finite field L of odd characteristic p, usually with q = |L|, and that exponents are considered modulo q - 1.
The surrounding paper context is about power maps/permutations, so if you keep 'invertible exponent' you should state gcd(s, q - 1) = 1 explicitly.
The draft omits the exact quantifier on v: the nice condition concerns the set of values N(1,v) as v ranges over L.
The paper distinguishes 'nice exponent' from a stronger 'Delta-differential exponent' condition; your draft does not mention that nearby context.
The phrase 'not equivalent to 1' is left implicit; to make the prime-field experimental statement stand alone you would need the paper’s precise equivalence relation on exponents.
The prime-field observation for p < 5000 is numerical evidence in the discussion, not the official conjecture itself.
Your question broadens the paper by asking for a full classification over all finite fields of odd characteristic; the paper’s official conjecture is narrower.
refined_question: Let L be a finite field of odd characteristic p, let q = |L|, and let s be an invertible exponent over L (so gcd(s, q - 1) = 1). For u, v in L define N(u,v) to be the number of pairs (x,y) in L^2 satisfying x + y = u and x^s + y^s = v. Call s nice if the set {N(1,v) : v in L} has at most three distinct values. Must 2 always occur among these differential multiplicities; equivalently, if s is nice, must there exist v in L with N(1,v) = 2?
justification: The draft is aiming at the paper’s 'nice exponent' discussion, but it replaces the paper’s official conjecture with a stronger classification question. In the paper, the central open problem is Conjecture 1.1: a nice exponent in odd characteristic should have differential multiplicity 2. Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 are part of the introductory context explaining why this is the right sharp formulation and why, over prime fields, the only experimentally observed nontrivial nice exponents are the classical examples represented by s = 3 and s = q - 2. So the most paper-faithful stand-alone research question is the multiplicity-2 existence question, not a global classification of all nice exponents.
